name: Crystal deodorant (alum stone)
lead: Crystal deodorant, often sold as an alum stone or "rock crystal", is a block of potassium or ammonium alum, a hydrated double sulfate salt of aluminium, rubbed on damp skin to reduce underarm and foot odour.[1][2] It is marketed as a natural, fragrance-free alternative to conventional deodorants.

Alum has been used since antiquity, as a dye mordant and as a styptic, and in Island Southeast Asia powdered potassium alum (tawas) is a traditional scentless deodorant.[2] Despite being sold as aluminium-free in some marketing, alum is an aluminium compound, though chemically different from the aluminium salts in antiperspirants.[1]

Published literature on the products consists mainly of case reports of skin reactions, including irritant dermatitis and granulomatous dermatitis.[3][4] No controlled trials of effectiveness were found.
infobox: Potassium or ammonium alum, KAl(SO4)2 or similar[2]

paras: Alum is a group of hydrated double sulfates, with potassium alum the form usually meant. It dissolves in water, tastes astringent and acts as a mild acid.[2] Deodorant stones are usually used as a solid block, while powdered or liquid forms also exist; patents from the 1990s describe a rotating-base tube for dispensing solid crystal deodorant and a liquid form made by dissolving alum in water or water and ethanol.[5][6]

Herodotus mentioned Egyptian alum as a valuable trade good, and Pliny and Dioscorides described it. It was the most common medieval mordant and has long served as a styptic for shaving nicks.[2] Wikipedia describes crystal deodorants as inhibiting bacterial action, and notes that crystal deodorants have been found to be a weak skin irritant.[1]

A 1999 report in Cutis described two patients who developed irritant dermatitis of the underarms shortly after using an over-the-counter natural deodorant crystal containing alum, calling it a previously unreported reaction to an ancient agent with newfound popularity as an alternative health product.[3] A 2014 report in the International Journal of Dermatology described crystal deodorant-induced axillary granulomatous dermatitis.[4]

The US FDA's 2003 review found insufficient data to change the status of aluminium antiperspirants, and claims linking aluminium deodorants to breast cancer or Alzheimer's disease are reported by Wikipedia not to have reliable evidence.[1] These concern antiperspirants generally; no source examined alum stones specifically.
No controlled studies of effectiveness were found. Published human data consist of case reports of irritant and granulomatous dermatitis following use.[3][4]

card.summary: A block of alum rubbed on skin as a natural deodorant; ancient use, but published evidence is limited to irritation case reports.
card.note: Case reports of irritant and granulomatous dermatitis; still an aluminium compound.

quick.overview:
Crystal deodorant is a block of potassium or ammonium alum, rubbed on damp skin to reduce odour. Alum has been used for centuries, and powdered alum is a traditional deodorant in Southeast Asia.

No controlled trials of its effectiveness were found; the published literature is mostly case reports of skin reactions.
quick.mechanism: Alum is astringent and is described as inhibiting the bacterial action that causes underarm odour. It does not block sweat like antiperspirants.
quick.risks: Case reports describe irritant dermatitis and granulomatous dermatitis in the armpits. Alum is an aluminium compound, though a different form from antiperspirant salts.
